claims.text: Clef is a layer in the console's threat detection, across public traffic and not only sign-in: fixed rules watch counts of sign-in activity, mail spend, probed paths, 401 and 403 responses, and when a window crosses a trigger the console sends the decider (Clef, general domain) counts only and raises an operator alert with its threat verdict and the numbers. Clef detects and never enforces; the bot check, limits and budget do the blocking.

honesty_conditions.text: Sign-in never waits on or fails because of the decider: with the decider down, sign-in is unchanged and the numbers still reach the operator, marked as not assessed.

The decider receives derived counts only, never addresses, IPs, user agents, paths or any other visitor-supplied string, so a visitor can't write into its prompt or send personal data across the mesh.
Verdicts are checked against labelled windows, including a real group of guests behind one IP, before the alert is trusted, and its misses are recorded.
A budget hit or a burst always alerts, whatever the decider says, so a wrong 'genuine' can't hide abuse.
The threat detector's decider call receives derived counts only, never addresses, IPs, user agents, paths or any other visitor-supplied string; only the message validator in c30 sends a guest's line.

claims.text: Threat detection stays cheap and can't be driven by attackers. Counting per request is in memory, with no database write or network call. The detector's Clef call runs at most once per 15-minute window and at most 24 times a day, only after a rule triggers, with one call in flight and a 5 second timeout. The message validator in c30 has its own bounds.

honesty_conditions.text: A test driving 10000 requests in a window with a fake clock and fake decider sees at most 1 Clef call, a fixed-size counter state, and no added database writes on the request path.
